notes:
I found sources for every verse, but how much I found varies. Verses 1–8 have the most from verse-by-verse commentaries. For 9–12 I mostly had to rely on short search excerpts, because the full Pulpit Commentary page wouldn't load and the Enduring Word page cut off partway through verse 8.

**Gaps:** I found nothing from Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist/Wesleyan (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com) or Orthodox (oca.org) sources. I also found nothing from bibleodyssey.org or the NET Bible's translator notes. So there is no Wesleyan or Lutheran view below on whether the "many" of vv. 11–12 means everyone or only some.

---

## Whole chapter: who is the Servant?

- **Traditional Christian reading:** Precept Austin argues the passage describes one innocent person, not a guilty nation, who dies for the guilty. It identifies him as the Messiah, Jesus. No, the prophet wrote about an innocent individual, not a guilty nation. He made it crystal clear that this individual died for the sins of the guilty so that the guilty might go free. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-53-commentary
- **The pronouns:** Precept Austin quotes the ESV Study Bible. "I" is the LORD, "he" is the Servant, and "we" are people who need the Servant to carry their guilt. which is why the servant cannot be Israel or the pious within Israel. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-53-commentary
- **Reformed nuance (Ligonier):** This devotional says Jews take the Servant to be the nation of Israel, and that they are not wholly incorrect, although they miss the essential point. In its view the Suffering Servant is Israel, the ideal and perfect Israel—Jesus Christ. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/suffering-servant
- **Jewish reading (as these Christian sites describe it):** S. Lewis Johnson, quoted on Precept Austin, says the "Servant = Israel" view is the view of many of the later rabbis. Precept Austin also says the messianic interpretation of Isaiah 53 was held by Jewish rabbis till the twelfth century. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62031/ GotQuestions quotes a medieval rabbi, Moshe Kohen Ibn Crispin, who read the passage as being about the King Messiah. https://www.gotquestions.org/suffering-servant-Isaiah-53.html
- **Catholic:** Catholic Answers says early Church Fathers such as Justin Martyr saw these descriptions of a suffering servant being fulfilled in Christ's passion and death. https://www.catholic.com/audio/cot/why-jew-should-be-catholic Another Catholic Answers page says the passage prophesies his atoning death on behalf of the Jewish people and the whole world, and points readers to the Catechism (CCC 601, 608, 615, 623). https://www.catholic.com/qa/jesus-and-cyrus-in-isaiah

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik (Enduring Word) sees two things predicted here. First, how strange it seems that a disfigured, suffering Messiah brings salvation. Second, that many would reject him and not believe the "report." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-53/
- "The arm of the LORD" stands for God's power. Guzik says that power shows itself *through* a Messiah who looks weak. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-53/
- Utley calls "arm of the LORD" a human picture of God's action, here involving the ministry of the Servant. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/isaiah-53.html
- Church Fathers: Justin Martyr noted that "Lord, who has believed our report?" is worded as if announcing events which had already come to pass. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/01288.htm

**v. 2**
- A "tender plant" is weak and easily harmed, but Guzik says it is safe because it grows "before Him," in God's presence. He takes the "dry ground" to be the spiritually and politically barren setting of first-century Galilee. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-53/
- Guzik reads "no beauty" to mean Jesus was not especially good-looking, not that he was ugly. He warns against trying to make the gospel attractive through image and style. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-53/

**v. 3**
- Guzik says "man of sorrows" doesn't mean Jesus was always gloomy; he showed real joy (Luke 10:21). His sorrow was for others, never self-pity. Guzik also quotes Spurgeon on the many kinds of sorrow Jesus knew. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-53/
- Guzik says people turned away because the Messiah had no outward charm, which shows that people value looks more than God does. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-53/
- **Pentecostal word study:** Anthony Palma (Assemblies of God) argues the Hebrew words translated "sorrows" and "grief" really mean "pains" and "sickness." He notes the same words return in v. 4. https://ag.org/-/media/AGORG/Beliefs/DivineHealing/HealingandAtonement.pdf?la=en

**v. 4**
- Guzik says this verse is mainly about the Messiah carrying our *pain*, not yet our guilt: he took on our griefs as if they were his own. People were right that he was "stricken by God." Their mistake was that they didn't see *why*. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-53/
- Bible Hub's study page sees a substitution theme here: The servant bears the burdens of humanity's griefs and sorrows, indicating a substitutionary role. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/isaiah/53.htm
- **Where traditions differ (healing):** see v. 5.

**v. 5**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Guzik notes that "wounded" literally means "pierced through." He says the Messiah suffered *in our place*. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-53/
  - The Pulpit Commentary finds four separate statements in this verse that all Christ's sufferings were for us, and constituted the atonement for our sins. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-53.html
  - Gill explains that "stripe" literally means the black-and-blue mark a blow leaves. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/dby/isaiah/53-5.html
  - Bible Hub's notes say the "peace" here (shalom) means being made right with God. Peter applies Isaiah's words to healing from sin (1 Pet 2:24–25). https://biblehub.com/isaiah/53-5.htm
- **Where traditions differ: is physical healing "in the atonement"?**
  - *Pentecostal (Assemblies of God):* The AG's official statement of beliefs says Deliverance from sickness is provided for in the Atonement, and is the privilege of all believers (Isaiah 53:4,5; Matthew 8:16,17; James 5:14–16). The AG position paper grants that Isaiah and 1 Peter mainly mean healing from sin, but because v. 4 stresses sickness, it says the gospel covers both. It adds that healing will only be complete when Jesus returns. https://ag.org/Beliefs/Position-Papers/Divine-Healing
  - Palma (AG) is more cautious. He says we ought, therefore, to be cautious about trying to formulate a detailed theology of "healing in the Atonement." Even so, he holds that healing comes to us through the Cross. https://ag.org/-/media/AGORG/Beliefs/DivineHealing/HealingandAtonement.pdf?la=en
  - *Charismatic/evangelical (Guzik):* The verse covers both spiritual and physical healing, since Matthew 8 applies it to the body and 1 Peter 2 to sin. But full healing comes at the resurrection, not necessarily now. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-53/
  - *Reformed (Ligonier):* Whether healing is in the atonement is clear in terms of Isaiah 53: it is. But when that healing takes place is a matter of great debate. https://www.ligonier.org/learn/scripture/isaiah_53/?sort=scripture&type=question+and+answer
- **Debated popular teaching (word of faith / "claim your healing"):**
  - Guzik describes the view that, because "we are healed" is past tense, every believer is promised perfect health now, and any sickness means the promise wasn't claimed in faith. He rejects it. Salvation has past, present and future stages ("have been saved," "are being saved," "will be saved"), and healing does too. Christians shouldn't "claim" healing while ignoring their symptoms, but they should pray boldly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-53/
  - Sam Storms (writing for TGC) describes the same claim: If you're not healed, it's not because God doesn't will it, but because you don't believe it. He then asks whether Matthew 8 actually supports it. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/physical-healing-atonement/
  - Ligonier also mentions people who think Christians should never suffer sickness at all. https://www.ligonier.org/learn/scripture/isaiah_53/?sort=scripture&type=question+and+answer

**v. 6**
- Guzik says sheep are stubborn animals that wander off. Each of us has our own favourite sins, and we tend to excuse ours while condemning other people's. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-53/
- Guzik sees here the Father and Son working together at the cross: the Father judged our sin as it was laid on the Son. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-53/
- A Bible Hub sermon says the confession of sin turns almost into a song because of the line "the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all." https://biblehub.com/sermons/isaiah/53-5.htm

**v. 7**
- Guzik ties the silence to Jesus before his accusers (Mark 15:2–5). He stresses that "lamb to the slaughter" means Jesus was *silent*, not helpless: he stayed in control (John 10:18). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-53/
- Utley: This means the Servant did not attempt to defend Himself. He also says "like a lamb" points to sacrifice (John 1:29). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/isaiah-53.html
- The Pulpit Commentary compares "oppressed" to Israel under the Egyptian slave-drivers. It suggests "afflicted" is better translated "he abased himself" (humbled himself). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-53.html
- Church Fathers: Augustine contrasts this silence with Christ's second coming. Then he will speak not the voice of weakness, as though to be judged; but the voice of power, as though going to judge. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801068.htm

**v. 8**
- Guzik reads "who will declare His generation?" as referring to his imprisonment, and also to the fact that he died without children. He says this is the first clear statement in the passage that the Servant would *die*. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-53/
- Enduring Word sees this verse as more evidence that the Servant can't be Israel: As badly as Israel has suffered through the centuries, she has never been cut off from the land of the living. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-53/
- Darrell Bock (TGC) also says the Servant can't be the people or the faithful remnant, because he is said to be cut off from the people (Isa 53:8). https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/the-suffering-servant-and-isaiah-53-a-conversation-with-darrell-bock/ Utley makes the same point. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/isaiah-53.html
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that "My people" may mean God's people or the prophet's people, depending on whether God or Isaiah is speaking. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-53.html
- Church Fathers: Justin Martyr applied a related line to Christ's coming burial and resurrection. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/01288.htm

**v. 9**
- The Pulpit Commentary says the New Testament confirms the Servant's sinlessness (1 Pet 2:22; 2 Cor 5:21; 1 John 3:5). As no other man was ever without sin, it follows that the Servant of the present chapter *must* be Jesus. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-53.html
- Precept Austin uses this verse against the "Servant = Israel" reading: Isaiah never says Israel was innocent. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-53-commentary

**v. 10**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - The Pulpit Commentary says Christ's sufferings came from God's set plan (Acts 2:23), so they were "in some sort his doing." God was "pleased" in the sense that he was glad to see the Son give himself and people redeemed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/53-10.htm
  - Matthew Poole says God was the main cause of Christ's sufferings, while human sin was the reason they were deserved. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/53-10.htm
  - A Bible Hub sermon notes that the Hebrew word behind "pleased" doesn't have to mean enjoyment. It also explains the "guilt offering" (Leviticus 5–6) as making amends to God. https://biblehub.com/sermons/isaiah/53-10.htm
  - Utley says the Servant clearly dies (vv. 8, 9, 12), so "He will prolong His days" must refer to life after death! https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/isaiah-53.html
- **Where traditions differ (penal substitution):**
  - *Catholic:* Karlo Broussard (Catholic Answers) calls penal substitution common among Protestants of the Reformed tradition. He argues the verse doesn't support it. On his reading, God *allowed* the Romans to crush the Servant as part of his plan, rather than actively doing it himself; ancient writers often credited everything to God directly. He calls Christ's death a substitute but not a punishment: a loving sacrifice that pays our debt, like a rich friend paying someone else's fines. https://www.catholic.com/audio/scw/the-nature-of-jesus-atoning-sacrifice
  - *Within Protestant commentary:* StudyLight's collected comments on this verse show both positions. One line says The scripture nowhere says that Christ is his sufferings underwent the wrath of God. Another speaks of the Father's hand pressing on Christ with "divine wrath," and of real punishment "for the sin of all his elect." The excerpts don't make clear which writer said what, so I can't attribute them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/53-10.html
- **Translation differences:** The NET Bible renders the verse "the Lord desired to crush him and make him ill, once restitution is made." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/net/isaiah/53-10.html The 1917 Jewish translation (JPS) has "crush him by disease." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/jps/isaiah/53-10.html

**v. 11**
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that God himself is clearly the speaker in vv. 11–12. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-53.html
- Utley points out that "Righteous One" and "justify" come from the same Hebrew root. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/isaiah-53.html
- The Catholic-text page on Bible Hub links "justify many" to Matthew 20:28 ("a ransom for many"). https://biblehub.com/catholic/isaiah/53-11.htm
- **Catholic:** Broussard argues "he shall bear their iniquities" can't mean Christ became guilty or was condemned in our place. He calls the phrase a poetic way of describing Jesus' atoning sacrifice as vicarious atonement, which involves substitution but just not penal (vicarious = on our behalf). https://www.catholic.com/audio/scw/the-nature-of-jesus-atoning-sacrifice

**v. 12**
- Palma points out that the verb in "He bore [nasa] the sin of many" is the same one used of the scapegoat (Lev 16:22). He says it carries the idea of the Messiah dying for his people and not only for them but in their place. https://ag.org/-/media/AGORG/Beliefs/DivineHealing/HealingandAtonement.pdf?la=en
- S. Lewis Johnson (on Precept Austin) counts, by some reckonings, twenty-one statements of substitution in vv. 4–8 and 10–12. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-53-commentary
- Bock says Isaiah's picture points to God's final, decisive rescue of his people. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/the-suffering-servant-and-isaiah-53-a-conversation-with-darrell-bock/
